# Multimodal routing and scenarios with `r5r` {#sec-m4-r5r}

This chapter shows the complete workflow of a public transport scenario analysis: build
the network, compute the time matrix, edit the GTFS to represent an intervention, recompute
and compare. The example is Fortaleza.

Each step ends by saving its result in the `dados/projeto_final/` folder. These are the
files the final project (@sec-m5-projeto) reads to put together the Fortaleza accessibility report:

| File in `dados/projeto_final/` | Step | Content |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `isocronas.rds` | 4 | isochrones from 15 to 60 min from the Centre |
| `itinerario.rds` | 5 | a detailed itinerary, from Messejana to the Centre |
| `linhas_cortadas.rds` | 6 | the routes removed in the scenario |
| `comparacao.rds` | 7 | jobs accessible per hexagon, current and scenario |
| `carga.rds` | 8 | road network loading |

::: {.callout-important}
## The `r5r` blocks are not run when the site is built

They require **JDK 21** and a folder with the OpenStreetMap `.pbf` and the city's GTFS:
large files, which are not kept in the repository. The code is ready to run on your
machine, and the synchronous session material walks through these steps live. Preparing the folder
is described in @sec-m5.

The chapter's **tables, charts and maps** are run: they use the files that this same
code produced, run on the course author's machine, and the results Ipea publishes in
`aopdata` for Fortaleza.
:::

```{r}
# for the reference maps: the Fortaleza grid with Ipea's results,
# the same used in @sec-m4-acessibilidade
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

arquivo <- "dados/brutos/aop_fortaleza.rds"

if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  aop <- aopdata::read_access(
    city = "Fortaleza",
    mode = "public_transport",
    year = 2019,
    peak = TRUE,
    geometry = TRUE,
    showProgress = FALSE
  )
  saveRDS(aop, arquivo)
}

aop <- readRDS(arquivo) |>
  dplyr::filter(P001 > 0)

mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
options(java.parameters = "-Xmx2G")   # memory for the JVM, BEFORE loading the package
                                      # (2 GB is enough for Fortaleza; for a larger region, raise it)
library(r5r)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(accessibility)

# where each step saves its result, for the final project
dir.create("dados/projeto_final", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 1. Build the network

```{r}
#| eval: false
pasta <- "dados/brutos/fortaleza"
list.files(pasta)     # must contain one .osm.pbf and one or more GTFS .zip files

rede <- r5r::build_network(data_path = pasta)   # before version 2.3: setup_r5()
```

On the first run R5 builds a `.dat` file with the network. With the Fortaleza extract in the
module package, it takes about 2 minutes; with the whole Northeast extract, much longer, and it needs a lot of
memory. That is why the package has only the city's region.
On later runs, it reuses it. If the GTFS or the `.pbf` change, delete the `.dat` to force a
rebuild.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# check what went into the network
r5r::street_network_to_sf(rede)$edges |> nrow()
r5r::transit_network_to_sf(rede)$routes |> nrow()
```

This pair of lines is the check that prevents the most common frustration: running everything and finding out
at the end that the GTFS was not recognised: because it was unzipped, outside its
validity period, or malformed.

## 2. Origin and destination points

```{r}
#| eval: false
# aopdata's hexagonal grid (the aop object, from the start of the chapter) works well
# as the unit of analysis: one point at the centre of each populated hexagon
pontos <- aop |>
  sf::st_centroid() |>
  dplyr::transmute(id = id_hex,
            lon = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
            lat = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry()

nrow(pontos)
```

`r5r` requires exactly the columns `id`, `lon` and `lat`. Points that fall far from the network are
discarded with a warning. Check the count before and after.

Each populated hexagon becomes an origin and destination point. The grid, with the population of
each hexagon:

```{r}
# mapgl wants coordinates in degrees (EPSG:4326); only the map's columns, for the tooltip
populacao <- aop |>
  dplyr::select(id_hex, populacao = P001) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

cores_pop <- c("#F7F6F2", "#E7A07A", "#7A1F0F")
faixa_pop <- range(populacao$populacao)

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = populacao, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_fill_layer(
    id = "populacao", source = populacao,
    fill_color = mapgl::interpolate(column = "populacao", values = seq(faixa_pop[1], faixa_pop[2],
                                    length.out = 3), stops = cores_pop),
    fill_opacity = 0.75, tooltip = "populacao"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Population", values = faixa_pop, colors = cores_pop)
```

## 3. Travel time matrix

```{r}
#| eval: false
# a Saturday, within the GTFS validity period (03/04 to 03/07/2026). This GTFS only has
# Saturday and Sunday trips: on a weekday, r5r finds no bus and returns
# walking only, without an error (see the warning below)
partida <- as.POSIXct("2026-05-16 07:00:00", tz = "America/Fortaleza")

ttm <- r5r::travel_time_matrix(
  rede,
  origins      = pontos,
  destinations = pontos,
  mode         = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = partida,
  time_window       = 60,      # 60 departures, minute by minute
  percentiles       = c(50),
  max_walk_time     = 20,      # minutes of walking at each end
  max_trip_duration = 90
)

nrow(ttm)
head(ttm)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check that the GTFS has trips on the chosen day

The Fortaleza GTFS in the module package declares a weekday service in `calendar`, but
all the trips in `trips` are on Saturday or Sunday. On a Thursday, `r5r` finds no
bus: the matrix comes out with about 38 thousand pairs, all on foot, and no error appears. On Saturday, it comes out with
3.7 million. Before choosing the date, see which services have trips:

```{r}
#| eval: false
table(gtfstools::read_gtfs(file.path(pasta, "gtfs_fortaleza.zip"))$trips$service_id)
```

If the matrix with `TRANSIT` is the same size as one with `WALK` only, that is the problem.
:::

The parameters that change the result the most, and that must appear in the methodological note:

| Parameter | Effect |
|:--|:--|
| `departure_datetime` | peak × off-peak changes times and frequencies |
| `time_window` + `percentiles` | captures the variability of waiting; the 50th percentile is the usual one |
| `max_walk_time` | maximum access walk; 15–20 min is current practice |
| `max_trip_duration` | cuts the matrix and speeds up the calculation a lot |

Any indicator per hexagon comes out of the matrix. One of the easiest to read is the **time to the
nearest health facility**. It is what Ipea computed for Fortaleza, in the morning
peak, by public transport:

```{r}
aop_saude <- aop |>
  dplyr::mutate(tempo_saude = dplyr::if_else(is.finite(TMIST), TMIST, NA_real_))

mapview::mapview(dplyr::select(aop_saude, id_hex, tempo_saude), zcol = "tempo_saude", lwd = 0, alpha.regions = 0.8,
                 col.regions = grDevices::hcl.colors(10, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE),
                 layer.name = "Minutes to health care")
```

Click on the hexagons at the edge of the city: the highest times are where the public transport
network reaches worst, and not necessarily where there are fewer health centres.

## 4. Isochrones

```{r}
#| eval: false
# from Praça do Ferreira, in the Centre
centro <- data.frame(id = "centro", lon = -38.5267, lat = -3.7275)

iso <- r5r::isochrone(
  rede,
  origins = centro,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = partida,
  cutoffs = c(15, 30, 45, 60),
  time_window = 60,
  max_walk_time = 20
)

saveRDS(iso, "dados/projeto_final/isocronas.rds")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# the site does not run r5r: it loads the result that the block above saved
iso <- readRDS("dados/projeto_final/isocronas.rds")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
iso <- dplyr::arrange(iso, dplyr::desc(isochrone))   # the smaller bands on top

ggplot(iso) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(isochrone)), colour = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = -1, name = "minutes") +
  theme_void()
```

The isochrone is the module's most effective communication product: anyone understands "how far
you can get in 30 minutes".

## 5. Detailed itineraries

```{r}
#| eval: false
# from Messejana to Praça do Ferreira (the centre from the previous step)
messejana <- data.frame(id = "messejana", lon = -38.4920, lat = -3.8300)

det <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(
  rede,
  origins      = messejana,
  destinations = centro,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = partida,
  max_walk_time = 20,
  shortest_path = FALSE
)

saveRDS(det, "dados/projeto_final/itinerario.rds")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
det <- readRDS("dados/projeto_final/itinerario.rds")
```

Each row of `det` is a **leg** of a trip option: the walk to the stop, each
bus, the final walk. With `shortest_path = FALSE`, several options come back:

```{r}
det |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::select(option, segment, mode, route, segment_duration, wait, distance)
```

On the map, the first option, with one colour per mode. Hover over a leg to see the
bus route:

```{r}
opcao <- dplyr::filter(det, option == 1)
modos <- unique(opcao$mode)
cores_modo <- c(WALK = "#7A7A7A", BUS = "#2F6B9A", RAIL = "#C2542D", SUBWAY = "#7A1F0F",
                TRAM = "#E7A07A")[modos]

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = opcao, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_line_layer(
    id = "itinerario", source = opcao,
    line_color = mapgl::match_expr("mode", values = modos, stops = unname(cores_modo)),
    line_width = 5, tooltip = "route"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Mode", values = modos, colors = unname(cores_modo), type = "categorical")
```

When a result looks odd, this is where you find out why: an 18-minute walk
to the stop, a 25-minute wait, two transfers.

## 6. Editing the GTFS: the scenario

`gtfstools` lets you modify the public transport network to represent an intervention:
remove feeder routes, change frequencies, create a corridor.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(gtfstools)

gtfs <- gtfstools::read_gtfs(file.path(pasta, "gtfs_fortaleza.zip"))

names(gtfs)                 # tables: agency, routes, trips, stop_times, shapes...
nrow(gtfs$routes)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
# scenario: cut the routes with the least service, the quarter with the fewest trips in the GTFS
viagens <- gtfs$trips |>
  dplyr::count(route_id, name = "viagens")

cortadas <- viagens |>
  dplyr::filter(viagens <= stats::quantile(viagens, 0.25)) |>
  dplyr::pull(route_id)

length(cortadas)
saveRDS(cortadas, "dados/projeto_final/linhas_cortadas.rds")

gtfs_cenario <- gtfstools::filter_by_route_id(gtfs, route_id = cortadas, keep = FALSE)

c(rotas_antes = nrow(gtfs$routes), rotas_depois = nrow(gtfs_cenario$routes))

dir.create("dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario", showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(list.files(pasta, pattern = "\\.pbf$", full.names = TRUE),
          "dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario")
gtfstools::write_gtfs(gtfs_cenario, "dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario/gtfs_cenario.zip")
# the scenario's old network, if any, would ignore the new GTFS: delete it to rebuild
unlink("dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario/network.dat")
```

Other useful edits:

```{r}
#| eval: false
gtfstools::filter_by_route_type(gtfs, route_type = 3)           # buses only
gtfstools::filter_by_time_of_day(gtfs, from = "06:00:00", to = "09:00:00")
area_estudo <- sf::st_point(c(-38.527, -3.727)) |>              # 3 km around the Centre
  sf::st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_buffer(3000)
gtfstools::filter_by_spatial_extent(gtfs, geom = area_estudo)   # spatial crop
gtfstools::get_trip_speed(gtfs)                                  # commercial speed per trip
gtfstools::get_trip_geometry(gtfs, file = "shapes")              # route alignments as sf
```

## 7. Recompute and compare

The comparison starts from the accessibility of the current scenario. For Fortaleza, Ipea publishes the
number of jobs accessible within 60 minutes by public transport, which is exactly the
`atual` (current) indicator computed below. It is a **cumulative** measure; the accessibility chapter, in module 4
(@sec-m4-acessibilidade), explains it and the other measures.

```{r}
empregos_60 <- aop |>
  dplyr::select(id_hex, empregos_60 = CMATT60) |>
  sf::st_transform(4326)

cores_acesso <- c("#F6DCCB", "#2F6B9A", "#173A57")
faixa_acesso <- range(empregos_60$empregos_60)

mapgl::maplibre(style = mapgl::carto_style("positron"), bounds = empregos_60, height = "525px") |>
  mapgl::add_fill_layer(
    id = "empregos_60", source = empregos_60,
    fill_color = mapgl::interpolate(column = "empregos_60", values = seq(faixa_acesso[1],
                                    faixa_acesso[2], length.out = 3), stops = cores_acesso),
    fill_opacity = 0.8, tooltip = "empregos_60"
  ) |>
  mapgl::add_legend("Jobs within 60 min", values = round(faixa_acesso), colors = cores_acesso)
```

The scenario is computed with the edited network, and what matters is the **difference** between the two
maps.

```{r}
#| eval: false
rede_cenario <- r5r::build_network("dados/brutos/fortaleza_cenario")

ttm_cenario <- r5r::travel_time_matrix(
  rede_cenario, origins = pontos, destinations = pontos,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = partida,
  time_window = 60, percentiles = 50,
  max_walk_time = 20, max_trip_duration = 90
)

# population, jobs and income quintile of each hexagon
uso_solo <- aop |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::transmute(id = id_hex, populacao = P001, empregos = T001, renda = R002)

acesso <- function(m) {
  accessibility::cumulative_cutoff(
    travel_matrix = m, land_use_data = uso_solo,
    opportunity = "empregos", travel_cost = "travel_time_p50", cutoff = 60
  )
}

acesso_cenario <- acesso(ttm_cenario) |>
  dplyr::rename(cenario = empregos)

comparacao <- acesso(ttm) |>
  dplyr::rename(atual = empregos) |>
  dplyr::left_join(acesso_cenario, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(uso_solo, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    perda_abs = cenario - atual,
    # with no access today, there is nothing to lose: the percentage change is left empty
    perda_pct = dplyr::if_else(atual > 0, 100 * (cenario / atual - 1), NA_real_)
  )

saveRDS(comparacao, "dados/projeto_final/comparacao.rds")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
comparacao <- readRDS("dados/projeto_final/comparacao.rds")
```

How much each income bracket loses, on average, weighting by population (quintile 1 is the lowest
income):

```{r}
comparacao |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    pessoas = sum(populacao, na.rm = TRUE),
    perda_media_pct = weighted.mean(perda_pct, populacao, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = renda
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(renda)
```

The expected result of this kind of scenario is a loss of accessibility concentrated on the
outskirts and in the lowest income strata. That is precisely the argument the analysis
serves to quantify, rather than assert.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
mapa_comparacao <- aop |>
  dplyr::left_join(comparacao, by = c("id_hex" = "id"))

ggplot(mapa_comparacao) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = perda_pct), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#b3402a", mid = "grey95", high = "#1a5b8a",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "Change (%)") +
  labs(title = "Impact of cutting the routes with the least service",
       subtitle = "Change in jobs accessible within 60 min by public transport") +
  theme_void()
```

## 8. Network assignment: `flownet` and `stplanr`

Module 3's desire lines show volume between pairs. To show the volume **on the
infrastructure**, each pair must be routed and the flows added up per segment:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# route 1: route the pairs with r5r and sum by segment with stplanr
# example pairs: from the 30 most populous hexagons to the 10 with the most jobs;
# the flow splits the origin's population among the destinations, by jobs
origens  <- aop |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::slice_max(P001, n = 30) |> dplyr::select(id_hex, P001)
destinos <- aop |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::slice_max(T001, n = 10) |> dplyr::select(id_hex, T001)

pares_od <- expand.grid(origem = origens$id_hex, destino = destinos$id_hex,
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(origem != destino) |>
  dplyr::left_join(origens, by = c("origem" = "id_hex")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(destinos, by = c("destino" = "id_hex")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(fluxo = P001 * T001 / sum(destinos$T001))

rotas <- r5r::detailed_itineraries(
  rede,
  origins      = pontos[match(pares_od$origem, pontos$id), ],
  destinations = pontos[match(pares_od$destino, pontos$id), ],
  mode = "CAR",
  departure_datetime = partida,
  shortest_path = TRUE
) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(pares_od, origem, destino, fluxo),
                   by = c("from_id" = "origem", "to_id" = "destino"))

carga <- stplanr::overline(rotas, attrib = "fluxo")

saveRDS(carga, "dados/projeto_final/carga.rds")

# route 2: flownet, estimation and assignment of flows on a network
# remotes::install_github("SebKrantz/flownet")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
carga <- readRDS("dados/projeto_final/carga.rds")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
carga <- dplyr::arrange(carga, fluxo)      # the most loaded segments on top

ggplot(carga) +
  geom_sf(aes(linewidth = fluxo), colour = "#1a5b8a", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.2, 3), name = "Flow") +
  theme_void()
```

The result is the **network loading**: the map in which the width sits on the road, not
in the air. It is the product that speaks directly to capacity planning. It is the natural starting
point for a bottleneck study.
